(p-99) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Humazah (the Slanderer, the Backbiter)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker.﴾

There has been disagreement about the meaning of the word "wayl" (woe).

It was said: it is a valley in Hell (Jahannam).

And it was said: it is a word of punishment and destruction.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had already mentioned these two meanings in Surat al-Jathiyah, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Woe to every sinful liar﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 7]. He explained that it is a verbal noun (masdar) with no verb of its own from which it derives, and that what permits beginning a sentence with it, although it is indefinite, is that it occurs in the context of invoking destruction upon them.

May Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, he favoured this meaning.

Among what supports the meaning he favoured is what came concerning the people of the garden that had become like a harvested field: when they saw it, they said: ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Anbiya': 14]. So it is a word said at the onset of calamities and when condemning.

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said: The origin of "wayl" is a word expressing anger and blame. Its original form is "wayy li-fulan" (alas for so-and-so), then it became common in their speech and was joined with the lam. It is said that "wayh" with the letter ha' is used to express compassion. End of quotation.

Also supporting al-Razi's view is the saying of Qarun: ﴿Ah, it is as if Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it.﴾ [al-Qasas: 82]

Similar to it, for expressing astonishment, is His saying: ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man?"﴾ [Hud: 72]

And His saying: ﴿He said, "Woe to me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal my brother's corpse?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31]

(p-100) The apparent meaning, then, is that it is a word said at times of severe distress and destruction, or at extreme astonishment at something resembling what is deemed unlikely.

What the Qur'an supports is this meaning. The cause of the disagreement may return to the fact that it occurs sometimes unrestricted, as in His saying: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 15], and here: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker.﴾

It also occurs together with mention of what is threatened, as in His saying: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, because of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 27], and His saying: ﴿So woe to those who wronged, from the punishment of a painful Day﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 65], where He mentions the Fire and the painful punishment.

Likewise His saying: ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, because of a witnessing of a great Day﴾ [Maryam: 37]. In all of this it is for severe warning, given what is mentioned along with it of the Fire, the painful punishment, and the witnessing of a great Day. It is not intended for its own sake apart from what is mentioned with it. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

His saying: ﴿scorner, mocker﴾. It was said: both have the same meaning, which is backbiting (ghibah).

Ibn Jarir recited the verse of Ziyad al-A'jam:

"You offer me your affection when you meet me, while lying, but when I am absent, you are the scorner, the slanderer."

He attributed this to Ibn 'Abbas, and it is one who strikes people and reviles them.

The Qur'an uses each of the two words separately from the other, in a way that indicates difference.

Concerning "humazah" (scorner) there is His saying: ﴿And do not obey every constant swearer, contemptible, going about slandering, hindering the good, transgressing, sinful﴾ [al-Qalam: 10-12] (wait, as stated) — indicating lying and tale-bearing (namimah).

Concerning "lumazah" (mocker) there is His exalted saying: ﴿And do not defame one another, nor call each other by offensive nicknames﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11].

And His saying: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58], which indicates that it is closer to disparagement and faultfinding in the presence of the person, not in his absence. Thus the two words differ in meaning and in description. Combining them is combining two ugly traits, so he deserved this severe warning with the word "wayl."

It has been said: "humz" is with the hand, and it was said: with the tongue in the presence of others, while "humz" in absence is backbiting.

(p-101) It was also said: "humz" is with the hand, "lumz" is with the tongue, and "ghamz" is with the eye. All these meanings are close, sharing in belittling others.

The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Who has gathered wealth and counted it﴾.

This description indicates that it is a cause (ʿillah, a reason or ground) for what precedes it, since the relative clause here serves as a substitute (badal al-kull, a substitute for the whole) for the preceding description. The fault lies not in "gathered wealth" but in "counted it, ﴿thinking that his wealth will make him immortal﴾." Regarding "ʿaddadahu" there are several meanings:

It has been said: he counted it again and again, guarding it.

It has been said: he counted it, meaning he hoarded it.

It has been said: he counted it, meaning he prepared it for future need.

It has been recited as "jammaʿa wa-ʿaddada" with shaddah (emphatic doubling) and without it. What is meant is the one who does not pay Allah's right in it, out of stinginess and miserliness, as was discussed previously in the surah ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase has diverted you﴾.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 104, verse 3:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal.﴾

This reckoning (husban) is the blameworthy thing, and it is upon it that the threat falls, because he disbelieved in the Resurrection (al-ba'th). Just as the owner of the garden said in Surah al-Kahf: ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish,"﴾ ﴿"And I do not think that the Hour will ever come to be."﴾ [al-Kahf: 35-36].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 104, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay! He will surely be thrown into the Huttamah.﴾ "Nay" (kalla) is a rebuke and a deterrent to him for his false assumption. "He will surely be thrown" (la-yunbadhanna) is the answer to an omitted oath, which is indicated by His saying "Nay."

This is explained by what preceded it in His saying: ﴿Then his mother will be the Abyss [Hawiyah].﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 9], meaning: he will be thrown with a throw, so he will plunge headlong upon the top of his head. We seek refuge in Allah.

Al-Huttamah (al-Huṭama): it is on the pattern fu'alah from al-hatm (al-ḥaṭm), which is breaking, then eating in large quantity.

It has been explained by what follows it: ﴿the Fire of Allah, kindled﴾ [al-Humazah: 6], and it was named "Huttamah" because it breaks everything cast into it, and it says: ﴿Is there any more?﴾

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 104, verse 8:

(p-102) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾ ﴿in extended columns﴾.

It has been said: "closed over them" refers to the columns, in that the columns become a closure for the door, like a lock and a bolt for it.

It has also been said: "in columns" means that they enter into columns like a reed hollow on the inside.

It has also been said: "in columns" means that their feet are placed in the columns in the form of shackles on an extended piece of wood, to which a number of people are fastened by their feet.

I had heard from the Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on us and on him, concerning this: that "columns" in the sense of a hollow reed, which is narrowed upon them, as in His saying: ﴿And when they are thrown into it, in a narrow place, bound together, they will call out there for destruction﴾ [al-Furqan: 13].

So this meaning is more preferable.

He also stated this explicitly in his dictation, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on us and on him.
